definition: Archaic means belonging to an earlier period of time and no longer in everyday use.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word archaic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know archaic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Much of his vocabulary felt archaic, so tied to his own century that Priya sometimes had to guess at his meaning.
An outdated bus schedule is much weaker than archaic — it is only a little behind the times, and one quick reprint makes it useful again.
An old-fashioned handwritten thank-you note is weaker than archaic — it feels quaint and charming, but people still happily write and receive them today.

Ancient means extremely old — often thousands of years old — and speaks only to age. Archaic is about use, not age alone: an archaic word or custom belongs to an earlier era and has dropped out of current practice. A mountain is ancient, but it cannot be archaic, because it was never something people used.

Obsolete means discarded because something newer replaced it, like floppy disks. Archaic points to an earlier era of history rather than to replacement by an upgrade: archaic laws or spellings belong to a vanished period. A gadget from last decade can be obsolete without being archaic — nothing about it belongs to a distant age.

Antiquated is a disapproving word for what is old-fashioned and no longer works well, like an antiquated filing system that slows an office down. Archaic is more neutral and scholarly: it places a thing in a vanished historical era without complaining about it. Scholars prize archaic manuscripts; no one prizes an antiquated system.

Archaic means belonging to an earlier period of time and no longer in everyday use.
In her grandmother's attic, Maya found archaic letters written in a spidery hand, words she'd never seen before because the language itself had changed so much.
Archaic means something is not just old, but old and no longer in everyday use — more precise than "ancient," which speaks to age alone.
A thing can survive in one narrow corner, like a legal contract or an old hymn, and still be archaic: what matters is that it has left ordinary use.
And archaic mostly describes language, customs and styles rather than objects still in service — a farmhouse people still live in is old, not archaic.
These letters belong to a vanished era of language, and that is exactly what archaic captures.
Archaic is a scholarly word for things that belong to a vanished past.

In everyday speech, say 'old-fashioned' or 'outdated.' Use archaic mainly for vocabulary, customs, or styles that clearly belong to a historical era — not for an object, however old, that is still in service.

Tracing her family's farm across an 1843 county map, Elena kept stumbling over villages she could not find in any modern atlas.
The settlements still existed; only their names had moved on.
The map's labels were archaic, recording what each place was called before the railway companies renamed whole districts to suit their timetables.
Locals had not spoken the old names in four generations, and the road signs Elena passed that afternoon bore no trace of them.
Only in the parish registers, and on maps like hers, did the older names survive at all.
